Further information:
This is a brief overview of the Zuma years in which we take a look at the rise and fall of Jacob Zuma as president. We look at how he managed to get into such a powerful position and how he managed to hang on to it despite so many attempts to remove him from power. We alos give a brief analysis of this past week's events and take a look at the role of Cyril Ramaphosa in the whol saga. We use analysts as well as people who worked closely with Zuma to gain insight in the processes and character of the man.

Press Release:


The Zuma Years
For years, President Jacob Zuma has been dogged by allegations of deception, corruption, and nepotism. He insists he’s done nothing wrong and believes he still enjoys the support of all South Africans, but pressure is mounting on the ruling ANC to force Zuma to resign. After a tumultuous ride and as the wheels continue to come off, Carte Blanche tracks a near decade under the Zuma Presidency.


Script:


Images: Zuma being sworn in
Link:
That was on the 9th of May 2009. A new President, a fresh start. Hope for a better future. But fast forward to April 2016. Then we hear the following from the highest court of the land about this very man: “The President thus failed to uphold, defend and respect the Constitution as the supreme law of the land.”
V/O:
A scathing indictment by the Constitutional Court. A failed President. A shattered dream. But that is not all says
Political analyst Prince Mashele.
Prince:
Under Zuma, unemployment has reached the highest level since 13 years. More South Africans are unemployed under Zuma. These are statistics and I am not manufacturing them. Number 2, under Zuman more South Africans are living in poverty. More that 50%. The level of poverty has gone up. Under Zuman South Africa was downgraded to junk by international ratings agencies. Under Zuman SOEs have collapsed. Eskom as we speak is bankrupt.
V/O:
Mavuso Msimang, is an ANC stalwart and former leader in Umkhonto weSiswe, agrees with Mashele’s take on Zuma.
Msimang:
The Jacob Zuma years as president of the country, they have been disastrous years, without any doubt.
V/O:
All of this is a far cry from the optimism that so many had when Zuma stepped into the presidency. (Siphiwe Sebeko, Reuters)
Vavi:
He was a people’s man. He came from a rural background, he had no chance to go to formal education, therefore issues of education, of poverty, of inequality of jobs, of proper healthcare that is affordable is much closer to his heart.
V/O:
Zwelinzima Vavi is the former General Secretary of the Congress of South African trade Unions and fought hard to get Zuma elected as President in 2009. He had high hopes for the man, but like so many others he was sorely disappointed.
Vavi:
He fooled us into believing that he was a workers’ hero, and we believed this nonsense that he was the champion of the workers’ class, and so let’s push for him. What a monumental error and mistake. He has proven for hard experience that he doesn’t have time for all those things.
V/O:
But who is this President who held so much promise and disappointed so deeply?

Jacob Gedleyihlekisa Zuma was born on 12 April 1942 in rural Kwazulu-Natal. He joined the ANC when he was 17 and became an activist. He was arrested in 1963.
Msimang:
Zuma went to Prison on Robben Island for 10 years. That showed a commitment to the struggle for the liberation of this country.
V/O3
In 1975 he went into exile, actively working for the ANC until 1990. In exile Zuma was also the Chief of the Intelligence Department of the ANC. For many it represents solid struggle credentials. But not all agree about this.
Prince:
Zuman has always been a criminal. His conduct underground in the ANC was actually criminal. There are allegations that when he was head of Intelligence he actually facilitated the disappearance, even the killing of his comrades. Some of which were innocent, accusing them of being apartheid spies and so on. So the criminal streak of Zuma has always been there.
V/O:
After the unbanning of the ANC in 1990 processes were put into place to turn a liberation movement into a political party, with mixed success.
Prince:
What the ANC failed to do during the transition that is after the unbanning, was to put into place a rigorous screening mechanism to screen its activists. Because they failed to do so there are many criminal elements, including Zuma, who actually fell through the cracks and made it to the upper echelons of the ANC.
V/O:
Zuma was very popular and had an enthusiastic following. He became Deputy President of the ANC in 1997 and in 1999 he was sworn in as deputy President of South Africa.
LINK:
But despite the optimism, Zuma was off to a really rocky start even before he became President.
Masimang:
In was in 2005 already he was implicated in a corruption scandal. Shabir Shaik He was sentenced to 15 years because he was accused of having corrupted Jacob Zuma. SAHO
V/O:
Shortly after then President Mbeki dismissed Zuma as Deputy President. In 2006 and 2007 Zuma was charged, first with rape and then with 783 charges of corruption and racketeering. He was acquitted of the rape charge and eventually the other charges were also dropped.

Despite this cloud, he was elected ANC President in 2007 with a huge majority over Thabo Mbeki and this lead to him being sworn in as President of South Africa in 2009.

Soon after he came to power Zuma started to manoeuvre his supporters into key positions and got rid of many senior ANC members. Some call it the Juniorization of the cabinet.
Vavi:
Before you know it you had all the juniors – Fikile Mabalula, Gigaba, Nonvula Mkonyama, Faith Muthambi, Zwane, Des van Rooyen, juniorised junioralised. All of them saying Baba, when they talk to him, Baba, and he gives them patronage.
V/O:
This enabled him to control many of the Government Departments and State Owned Enterprises. This in turn allowed corruption and incompetence to thrive in the way we have seen at SAA, The SABC, Escom, PRASA, Transnet, PetroSA, to name but a few. It drained hundreds of billions of rand from the fiscus, enriched Zuma sympathizers and eventually resulted in South Africa being downgraded to junk status by rating agencies.

Zuma himself staggered from one scandal to the next during his tenure:

In 2013 his friends the Guptas are allowed to use Waterkloof as a private air strip for a wedding.

In 2014 the Public Protector releases a damning report on unlawful upgrades at Zuma’s compound in Nkandla which is later upheld by the Constitutional Court.

In December 2015 he dismisses Finance Minister Nene, replacing him with Des van Rooyen. It results in the Rand plummeting and billions of rands being withdrawn from the JSE. (Courtesy Mail and Guardian)

In November 2016 the State of Capture report is released, despite Zuma’s efforts to stop it.

In October 2017 the Supreme Court of Appeal rules that the decision not to prosecute Zuma was wrong and opens the way for the 783 counts of corruption against Zuma to be re-instated.

Since 2015 there have been four votes of no-confidence in Zuma. He has survived them all, but significantly in 2017 a number of ANC MP’s for the first time voted against Zuma.

All of this resulted in a whole nation starting to demand that he steps down.

In December 2017 Cyril Ramaphosa replaces Zuma as President of the ANC and in 2018 he calls on Zuma to resign.

This past week various ANC structures, as well as Ramphosa have asked Zuma to resign. He still refuses.

V/O:
The big question of course is, how does Zuma manage to resist all these attempts to get rid of him?
Prince:
You have the Zuman faction in al the structures of the ANC. He knows that he remains the commander of that group. It is a criminal battalion, reporting to the top criminal who is Zuma. ……to criminal who is Zuma.
V/O:
And they continue to support him. This Zuma faction was only narrowly defeated by Cyril Ramaphosa in December.
Prince:
So, Cyril Ramaphosa is leading a faction as well that reports to him. So, you are having a battle of factions. So, when Zuma says I’m going nowhere, he knows he has got his own battalion in the leadership of the ANC that is going to fight for him. That is why it has been difficult to deal with Zuma. So South Africans must not expect decisiveness from the leadership of the ANC, because essentially there is not one ANC. There are two ANC’s within the ANC.
V/O:
However, there is also another reason why it is not a simple matter to get rid of a sitting President. And this can frustrate parties who want to act.
LINK:
Every 5 years the ANC has a national conference. At this Conference they elect a new National Executive Committee which is the highest organ of the ANC between conference. They have the power to appoint somebody to be elected as President of the country.
V/O:
The actual election of the person to President is done by Parliament, and he or she answers to Parliament. The NEC can recall the person, that is asking him or her to step down as President. But that is about it. The sitting President can refuse, as in Zuma’s case. Then the ANC’s hands are tied. Only Parliament can actually make him go.
LINK
And with so many calls to step down over such a long period, the question must be asked: why has the man clung on to power for so long?
Prince:
He wants to hold on to power to protect his own skin, because he knows the day he is out of power and there is a new guy, that new guy might appoint a permanent Head of Police with credibility, a permanent Head of the NPS with credibility. That would facilitate Zuma’s going to jail.
V/O:
Despite delaying tactics and negotiations that has led nowhere, it seems that Ramaphosa’s side is slowly gaining a majority.
Msimang:
The ANC has now come to a point where for the first time, for the first time, I think a majority of their members have been able to say to Jacob Zuma: “You must go”.
V/O:
But that does not mean the ANC has been purged of corrupt elements.
Prince:
Thabo Mbeki was removed by dodgy characters, by criminals in the ANC. They were all dodgy. They ganged up and got rid of him. Who says the criminals in the ANC cannot gang up and get rid of Cyril Ramaphosa. By the way, Cyril Ramaphosa is the weakest leader of the ANC. He won by a whisker -- under 200 votes. If these criminals were to gang up, by the way they can actually call a special conference and remove Cyril Ramaphosa. The law is very weak in the face of the power of the criminal network in the ANC….. and that is scary!

Prince: He wants to hold on to power to protect his own skin, because he knows the day he is out of power and there is a new guy, that new guy might appoint a permanent Head of Police with credibility, a permanent Head of the NPS with credibility. That would facilitate Zuma’s going to jail. V/O: Despite delaying tactics and negotiations that has led nowhere, it seems that Ramaphosa’s side is slowly gaining a majority. Msimang: The ANC has now come to a point where for the first time, for the first time, I think a majority of their members have been able to say to Jacob Zuma: “You must go”. V/O: But that does not mean the ANC has been purged of corrupt elements. Prince: Thabo Mbeki was removed by dodgy characters, by criminals in the ANC. They were all dodgy. They ganged up and got rid of him. Who says the criminals in the ANC cannot gang up and get rid of Cyril Ramaphosa. By the way, Cyril Ramaphosa is the weakest leader of the ANC. He won by a whisker -- under 200 votes. If these criminals were to gang up, by the way they can actually call a special conference and remove Cyril Ramaphosa. The law is very weak in the face of the power of the criminal network in the ANC….. and that is scary!
